content: Referrals for further testing to diagnose tuberculosis (TB) disease and infection, as well as evaluations, should be conducted in accordance with national guidelines. Healthcare workers, community health workers, and other service providers should undergo systematic training and on-the-job capacity building to enhance their ability to screen for TB symptoms effectively. Job aids should be developed to outline the steps for ruling out TB disease. Access to chest radiography should be organized through public or private health facilities or mobile vans, as required by national policy. This may involve agreements with private hospitals and radiologists or the provision of free vouchers for individuals to access private services. Standard tools for data collection should be developed or existing tools (e.g., patient files and electronic records) updated to include relevant data on active case finding (ACF) and activities to rule out TB disease. The national health management information system (HMIS) should summarize data at key steps in the care cascade and report program performance indicators to the national level. Effective TB symptom screening forms the foundation of TB preventive treatment (TPT) services. Additional diagnostic tests, such as those for TB infection, chest radiography, and other diagnostic methods, may be utilized. Key steps in ruling out TB disease and considering TPT include screening adults and adolescents living with HIV, children living with HIV, HIV-negative household or close contacts of TB patients, and other clinical at-risk populations. Symptom-based screening should include signs such as cough, fever, weight loss, night sweats, or other relevant symptoms. Screening should occur at every health facility visit or contact with a health worker. Chest radiography, while not mandatory, is desirable in certain populations, such as people living with HIV (PLHIV) on antiretroviral therapy (ART) or asymptomatic adolescent and adult contacts, where resources and capacity allow. If a screening test is positive, diagnostic testing for TB should follow, with rapid diagnostics like Xpert MTB/RIF or urine lipoarabinomannan (LAM) assays recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) or national guidelines. Testing for TB infection, such as tuberculin skin tests (TST) or interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA), is not required for PLHIV or contacts under five years of age. However, in other populations, these tests can help avoid unnecessary treatment of uninfected individuals, particularly in low-prevalence settings. The absence of testing should not prevent the provision of TPT to those in need. Contraindications to TPT include active hepatitis (acute or chronic), regular and heavy alcohol consumption, symptoms of peripheral neuropathy, concurrent use of hepatotoxic medications (e.g., nevirapine), or a history of hypersensitivity to TPT. Pregnancy or a previous history of TB are not contraindications. Counseling should provide information on TB infection, the need for TPT, medication schedules, adherence support, follow-up visits, benefits of completing treatment, potential adverse events, and actions to take if TB symptoms or adverse events occur. Screening for children and pregnant or breastfeeding women can be integrated into maternal and child health services, immunization clinics, and nutrition clinics. For PLHIV, ACF and TPT should be integral components of care packages, especially in differentiated HIV service delivery models. Governments and donors should invest in health system capacity, including human resources, logistics, and monitoring and evaluation, to support TST and IGRA testing and avoid unnecessary TPT and related harms. Testing for TB infection is not mandatory for TPT introduction and scale-up. However, where testing is recommended, it should target at-risk groups, such as clinical risk groups, contacts over five years of age, prisoners, and healthcare workers. Testing helps identify individuals at high risk for TB infection or disease progression, ensuring appropriate evaluation and treatment. The choice of TPT regimen should consider individual circumstances, resource availability, and patient preferences. WHO recommends several options for latent TB infection (LTBI) treatment, including six or nine months of daily isoniazid, three months of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, three months of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin, one month of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid, or four months of daily rifampicin alone. Shorter rifamycin-based regimens are associated with better adherence and fewer adverse events. The 2020 WHO guidelines broaden the applicability of TPT regimens across all TB burden settings, provided the country or treatment site can reliably rule out TB disease before starting TPT and has the resources to implement TPT properly.
